entities.name: United States Constitution
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The United States Constitution, ratified on June 21, 1788 and implemented on March 4, 1789, serves as the foundational legal document of the United States, establishing the framework of the national government and delineating the rights of citizens. Drafted during the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia, it was primarily authored by James Madison, who is often referred to as the 'Father of the Constitution.' This document not only marked the beginning of a new era in governance but also influenced democratic movements worldwide, symbolizing the emergence of a republic based on the principles of liberty and justice.

The Constitution arose from a critical need to replace the Articles of Confederation, which had proven inadequate in unifying the states and managing national affairs. The Constitutional Convention brought together 55 delegates, including key figures like George Washington and Benjamin Franklin, who debated and crafted a framework that included the separation of powers, checks and balances, and the Bill of Rights, ratified in 1791. The document has been amended 27 times to adapt to changing societal needs, reflecting its foundational role in American law and governance.

The legacy of the United States Constitution extends far beyond its borders, as it has inspired countless democratic movements globally and provided a model for numerous constitutions around the world. Its principles of democracy, rule of law, and individual rights have influenced legal frameworks in nations such as Germany, Japan, and South Africa. The Constitution has also become a living document, often interpreted by the Supreme Court, shaping American law and culture through landmark decisions that continue to resonate in contemporary society.
